claims.text: A high density of fine, stable grain boundaries promotes formation of a multicomponent passivating oxide layer.
The passivating oxide layer rapidly self-heals after mechanical damage.
The passivating oxide suppresses corrosion by blocking corrosive attack at damage sites.
Fine, stable grain boundaries help suppress wear by accommodating localized deformation.
A fine-grained microstructure has a greater proportion of high-energy grain boundaries.
High-energy grain boundaries serve as preferential nucleation sites for a protective multicomponent oxide.
The protective oxide can reform under mechanical wear.
Oxide reformation during wear reduces exposure of the underlying alloy to corrosive attack.
The oxide improves abrasive-damage resistance by arresting crack initiation and propagation.
A fine-grained, high-grain-boundary alloy will have lower wear volume than a matched coarse-grained alloy during simultaneous wear-corrosion testing.
A fine-grained, high-grain-boundary alloy will have a lower corrosion rate than a matched coarse-grained alloy during simultaneous wear-corrosion testing.
The combined degradation rate will be lower than the sum of the rates measured under separate wear-only and corrosion-only conditions.
A coarser microstructure has fewer grain boundaries and forms a less continuous or less robust passive oxide film.
The predicted protection requires an environment that supports passivation, including sufficient oxygen availability and moderate corrosivity.
The protective mechanism may fail in extremely reducing environments.
The protective mechanism may fail at mechanical stresses high enough to remove the oxide faster than it can reform.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis centers on a fine-grained, high-grain-boundary test alloy, but the stated initial material has only moderate grain size and the stated intervention is environmental exposure rather than grain refinement. The falsification design later introduces a refined sample, leaving the focal material state inconsistent across fields.
